prompt: Match each piece of blue team work to its kind.
"The defender must be right every time, the attacker only once." Where does the lesson say that is true?

choices.text: In prevention
choices.why: Right. One missed patch can be enough to get in.

choices.text: Everywhere, without exception
choices.why: The lesson says it is half true.

choices.text: Only in small shops like this one
choices.why: Size does not change the argument.

choices.text: In detection, since one missed alert is enough
choices.why: In detection the balance turns: the defender needs to notice one step.

choices.text: The red team's report after an exercise
choices.why: The SOC is on the blue side.

choices.text: A type of second factor used by administrators
choices.why: Unrelated to MFA.

choices.text: A standard for writing firewall rules
choices.why: It is a team, not a standard.

choices.text: A team that watches alerts
choices.why: Right. A security operations centre.

prompt: What separates a red team from a criminal?

choices.text: Red teams use gentler techniques
choices.why: The techniques can be the same.

choices.text: Red teams only test from inside the office
choices.why: They test from wherever the scope says.

choices.text: Red teams never find anything serious
choices.why: They often do; that is the point.

choices.text: Written permission and rules
choices.why: Right. Agreed before anything starts.

prompt: Match each description to the kind of red side work.

pairs.left: find as many weaknesses as possible in one application
test whether the organisation notices a realistic attack over weeks
referees who write the rules and decide what counts

prompt: Which of these belong in the rules of engagement? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: the passwords the testers will guess
choices.why: The rules govern conduct, not answers.

choices.text: the limits, such as no deleting data
choices.why: Even inside the scope.

choices.text: an emergency contact on each side
choices.why: And a way to stop everything.

choices.text: the scope: which systems and people may be targeted
choices.why: The first item.

prompt: A student wants to practise by testing a local shop's website without asking. What does the lesson say?

choices.text: It is a crime without written permission
choices.why: Right. Practise in a lab you own.

choices.text: Fine, if nothing is damaged
choices.why: Permission, not damage, decides legitimacy.

choices.text: Fine for small shops, since they have no security team
choices.why: Size changes nothing about the law.

choices.text: Fine, if the results are sent to the shop afterwards
choices.why: Telling them afterwards is not authorisation.

prompt: What changes when red and blue work as purple?

choices.text: The blue team is no longer told about the exercise
choices.why: The opposite: blue is in the room.

choices.text: The red team stops writing reports and leaves after a day
choices.why: Purple changes how they work together, not how long red stays.

choices.text: A third team takes over both jobs
choices.why: Purple is a way of working, not a third team.

choices.text: Each technique is followed at once by: was it seen?
choices.why: Right. Then change something and run it again.

prompt: Why does the lesson call a detection proved by purple work more durable than a list of holes?

choices.text: Somebody trying to get past it tested it
choices.why: Right. It says what an attacker would run into.

choices.text: Because purple teams use more expensive tools
choices.why: Cost is not the argument.

choices.text: Because lists of holes expire after a year by law
choices.why: No such law.

choices.text: Because detections cannot be bypassed once written
choices.why: They can; that is why they are tested.

prompt: What does the lesson call the cheapest security practice in the course?
hint: Try to get past what you built.

choices.text: After adding a control, try to beat it and read the logs
choices.why: Right. The purple idea at a small scale.

choices.text: Hiring an external red team every quarter
choices.why: That is far from cheap.

choices.text: Waiting for an incident and learning from it
choices.why: That is the most expensive way to learn.

choices.text: Buying a SOC service
choices.why: Useful, and not cheap.

prompt: How many 401 lines did grep -c count in the portal's log after the red step?
The red step got six 401s. What was the exercise's real question?

choices.text: Whether the login would hold
choices.why: Lesson 8 already showed it would; that was not the question.

choices.text: How long ana's password is
choices.why: The exercise used wrong passwords on purpose.

choices.text: Whether anything in the shop saw it
choices.why: Right. Seen, and could somebody act on it.

choices.text: Whether the firewall blocks the internet
choices.why: The portal answered every request.

prompt: Why does the missing time on each log line make the detection impossible?
hint: Six in two seconds, or six in a month.

choices.text: Guessing and forgetful users look the same
choices.why: Right. No rule can tell them apart without time.

choices.text: The 401 codes are wrong without a time
choices.why: The codes are right; the context is missing.

choices.text: Times are required by law in every log
choices.why: The lesson's reason is detection, not law.

choices.text: Without time the log cannot be read at all
choices.why: It can be read; it cannot separate the two cases.

prompt: Failed attempts log - instead of a username. What could the shop not see because of that?

choices.text: Which address the attempts came from
choices.why: The address is recorded; uniq -c counted it.

choices.text: Whether the portal was running
choices.why: Every request was answered and logged.

choices.text: How many attempts there were
choices.why: grep -c counted six.

choices.text: Attempts spread over every staff account
choices.why: Right. The claimed name has to be recorded, marked as claimed.

prompt: Match each measure to what it counts.

pairs.right: from the event to somebody knowing
how long an attacker was inside before being found

prompt: What is MITRE ATT&CK used for in this lesson?

choices.text: A tool that blocks attacks automatically
choices.why: It blocks nothing; it describes.

choices.text: The score given to a CVE
choices.why: That is CVSS, from lesson 2.

choices.text: A law requiring red team exercises
choices.why: It is a public catalogue, not a law.

choices.text: Mapping which techniques we would see
choices.why: Right. A map of where the defence is blind.

choices.text: A red team exercise nobody is told about
choices.why: Everybody at the table knows.

choices.text: A penetration test of the office furniture
choices.why: A play on the name, not the meaning.

choices.text: A spreadsheet of detection rules
choices.why: It is a conversation, not a document.

choices.text: Talking through an incident, step by step
choices.why: Right. It finds the gaps that show up under pressure.

prompt: Order the steps of the purple loop.
items: blue checks whether it was seen
if not, change a log or a rule
red runs the same technique again
trap: Running it again is what proves the change worked.
